title: Stream processing
subtitle: Count, sum and join events as they arrive. Learn event time, windows, watermarks and checkpoints, and what "exactly-once" really promises.

c.v: A ride app shows a live chart: rides started per minute, per city. A small job reads ride events from Kafka and counts them. Each count goes into the minute when the job reads the event.
One evening the job is down for 10 minutes during a deploy. Kafka keeps the events, so nothing is lost. When the job comes back, it reads the 10-minute backlog in about 30 seconds.
The chart shows 10 empty minutes, then one minute with about ten times the normal rides. A pricing rule watches that chart. It sees "demand spike" and raises prices across the city.
There was no spike. The rides happened at a normal rate. The job counted them by when it
read
them, not by when they
happened
. The team switches to the time inside each event. Then phones that were offline in a tunnel send their events 3 minutes late, and the team learns about late data.

A stream processor is a program that runs forever. It reads an endless flow of events, keeps some memory between them, and sends out results. Apache Flink, Kafka Streams and Spark Structured Streaming are the common tools.
Every event has two times.
Event time
is when it happened on the device.
Processing time
is when your machine sees it.
The gap between them changes all the time. Network delays, backlogs and offline phones can make it minutes, hours or days.
You cannot sum an endless stream, so you cut it into windows, like "each minute".
If you group by processing time, events land in the wrong window whenever the gap changes.
That is the ride chart bug.
Grouping by event time is correct, but raises a new question. When is the 12:00 minute
finished
? A late event could still arrive. A
watermark
is the engine's answer: a marker that says "event time has now reached t".
The key idea.
Group by when things happened, not when you saw them. A watermark decides when a window is done. Some events will still come late, so decide on purpose what to do with them.
Step through one window. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Windows
A
tumbling window
has a fixed size and never overlaps. Each event belongs to exactly one, like "12:00 to 12:01". A
sliding window
has a size and a slide. A 10-minute window that slides every 5 minutes overlaps, so one event can count in two windows. A
session window
closes after a gap with no events, for example 30 minutes without a click.
Watermarks and late data
A common rule is "newest event time seen, minus a fixed delay". Flink's built-in bounded out-of-orderness strategy follows this rule.
With a 5-second delay, a window ending at 12:01 fires soon after an event from 12:01:05 or later arrives.
An operator with many inputs uses the
smallest
watermark of them.
So one quiet Kafka
partition
can hold back the whole job. Flink's
withIdleness
setting marks such an input as idle so the rest can move on.
Pick the delay with care. A watermark that is too slow makes every result wait. One that is too fast closes windows early and turns normal events into late ones.
An event is late when it arrives after the watermark has passed its time.
For windows, what matters is the end of the window. Flink drops an event only if the watermark has already passed the end of its window plus the
allowed lateness
. The allowed lateness is 0 by default.

If you set it, an event that arrives within that time still joins its window, and the window can fire again with a new result. Flink keeps the window's state until the lateness runs out. After that, you can route even later events to a
side output
instead of losing them silently.
Kafka Streams calls the same idea a grace period. A record that arrives after it is discarded for that window.
Spark uses a watermark to know how late data can be, and to clean up old state.
Keyed state and where it lives
A count per city must be remembered between events. Flink keeps this
keyed state
next to the operator, split by key, so each update is local.
Kafka Streams also keeps local state stores, with automatic recovery.
Flink's default
state backend

keeps state as Java objects on the heap. It is fast, but limited by memory. The RocksDB backend keeps state on local disk, so it suits long windows and very large state. Each access must be serialized, and the docs call it "an
order of magnitude
slower" on average. RocksDB also supports incremental checkpoints.
Checkpoints: barriers in the stream
If a machine dies, the counts in memory are gone. So Flink takes regular snapshots, called checkpoints. The design is "inspired by" the Chandy-Lamport algorithm for distributed snapshots.
The 2015 paper behind it describes how, for a dataflow with no cycles, the snapshot needs only operator state, not the messages in flight.
It works like this.
The sources insert a
checkpoint barrier
into the stream and note their position, such as a Kafka
offset
Barriers never overtake records. Everything before barrier n belongs to checkpoint n.
An operator with two inputs waits until barrier n has come from both. This is called alignment. Then it passes the barrier on and saves its state.
When every sink has received barrier n and told the coordinator, checkpoint n is complete.
On a failure, Flink restores all state from the last complete checkpoint. It rewinds the sources to the saved offsets and reads again.
Note that checkpointing is off until you turn it on.
A
savepoint
is a checkpoint you trigger by hand. It does not expire when newer checkpoints finish.
You use it to stop a job, deploy new code, or change parallelism, then resume. Give each operator a stable ID with
uid()
, or the new version may not find its old state.
What "exactly-once" means here
Flink's
exactly-once
is about state. After a restore, records processed since the checkpoint have not touched the saved state.
But those records
are
processed again. A call to an outside API inside your code can run twice.
End-to-end exactly-once needs two more things. The source must rewind to the checkpoint position. The sink must take part, by committing writes in a
transaction
or by writing idempotently.
Spark says the same: replayable sources plus
idempotent
sinks.
Kafka Streams with
exactly_once_v2
covers reading from Kafka and writing results back to Kafka topics.
Uber's ad pipeline shows the cost. Flink writes results to Kafka in transactions that commit only at the next checkpoint, every 2 minutes. Readers use
read_committed

, so they see results only after the next checkpoint, which can be about 2 minutes later. Uber says the checkpoint interval is the main delay, so the pipeline is "not exactly 'real-time'". Uber also gives each record a unique ID, so its databases can upsert or deduplicate.
Backpressure
When a sink is slow, buffers fill and the slowness spreads back to the source. Barriers travel with the data, so they wait in the same queues.
Checkpoints then take much longer.
Flink offers two fixes. Buffer debloating keeps less data in flight. Unaligned checkpoints let barriers pass buffered data, but save that data in the checkpoint, which adds I/O.
Plain consumer + database
Each event is handled alone.
You write it yourself.
Copying, enriching or upserting each event. Simple to run.
Kafka Streams
Local state stores.
, with a grace period.
Kafka in, Kafka out, with exactly-once inside Kafka.
Apache Flink
Heap or RocksDB, with checkpoints.
, with watermarks, lateness and side outputs.
Large state and complex time logic. More moving parts to run.
Spark Structured Streaming
, with watermarks.
Teams already on Spark. Results come in small batches, for example every second.
Nightly batch job
n/a
n/a
Reports where a day of delay is fine. Easiest to fix and rerun.
Simple rule:
if each event can be handled alone, a consumer plus an idempotent write is enough. Reach for a stream processor when you need windows, joins over time, or large state per key.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask first:
"Which time are we grouping by?"
Business questions almost always mean event time.
Write down the watermark delay and the allowed lateness, and why. Then measure how late events really are.
Never drop late events silently. Send them to a side output with a counter and an alert.
Watch for a stuck watermark. One idle partition can stop every window from firing.
Turn checkpointing on, store checkpoints in durable storage, and set
uid()
on every stateful operator before the first deploy.
For every sink, ask:
"What happens when the last 2 minutes are replayed?"
Use a transactional or idempotent sink.
Choose the checkpoint interval as a
latency
budget, since transactional sinks only commit at checkpoints.
Use RocksDB when state may outgrow memory. Size the local disks for it.
"Here is our Flink job. List every operator that uses processing time. For each, tell me if the business question needs event time instead."
"Add a bounded out-of-orderness watermark of 10 seconds, idleness detection of 1 minute, allowed lateness of 2 minutes, and a side output for late events with a metric."
"Write a test that feeds events out of order into this windowed count, including one late and one very late event. Assert each window's output."
"Review this sink. If the job restarts from the last checkpoint, could any row be written twice? Show me how to make it idempotent."
The timestamp comes from a field in the event, not from
System.currentTimeMillis()
Late data goes somewhere you can see. The default drops it.
Side effects inside operators, such as HTTP calls, are safe to repeat.
Every stateful operator has a stable
uid()
, so a savepoint restore works after a code change.
The test really sends events out of order. A test with sorted input proves nothing about watermarks.
The agent did not "fix" late data by making the watermark delay huge. That only delays every result.

q.v: A job counts orders per minute using processing time. It was down for 10 minutes and then catches up in 30 seconds. What does the chart show?

options.v: The right count for every minute, because Kafka kept the events.
A gap of 10 minutes, then one minute with about 10 minutes of orders in it.
Nothing changes, because processing time ignores downtime.

why.v: Processing-time windows use the clock of the machine. All the old events are read in one minute, so they are all counted in that minute.

q.v: In Flink, what does a watermark with time 12:01:00 tell an operator?

options.v: That every event with a time up to 12:01:00 has been written to the sink.
That event time has reached 12:01:00, so no more events at or before that time are expected.

why.v: A watermark is a promise about event time, not about the clock. It can be wrong, which is why late events exist.

q.v: Your Flink job has exactly-once checkpointing on. It calls a payment API inside a map function. The job fails and restarts. What can happen?

options.v: Nothing. Exactly-once means each record runs exactly once.
Some payments are sent twice, because records after the last checkpoint are processed again.
Flink rolls back the payment API calls.

why.v: Flink restores state and replays input from the last checkpoint. Its state ends up as if each event counted once, but outside calls repeat.

q.v: What is the main reason to choose the RocksDB state backend over the heap backend?

options.v: It is faster for every state access.
Your state is too large for memory, for example long windows or many keys.
It is the only backend that supports checkpoints.

why.v: RocksDB keeps state on local disk, so it can hold much more. Each access must be serialized, so it is slower than the heap.

q.v: You need a Kafka consumer that writes each order to Postgres, keyed by order ID. There are no windows or joins. What do you use?

options.v: A plain consumer with idempotent upserts. A stream processor adds little here.
Flink with RocksDB and exactly-once checkpoints.
Spark Structured Streaming with a one-second trigger.

why.v: There is no state across events and no time logic. An upsert by order ID is already safe to repeat.
